title: Shopping
canDo: I can say any number from 100 to 100,000, getting さんびゃく, ろっぴゃく, はっぴゃく, さんぜん and はっせん right.
I can ask how much something costs (〜は いくらですか) and understand a price said in えん.

grammar.title: ひゃく・せん・まん (up to 100,000)
grammar.explanation:
Big numbers are built like the ones you already know: **[how many] + [unit]**. ひゃく = 100, せん = 1,000, まん = 10,000. にひゃく = 200, ごせん = 5,000, よんまん = 40,000. Then just join them, from the biggest unit to the smallest: にせん + ごひゃく + じゅう = にせんごひゃくじゅう (2,510).
• 100 is just ひゃく and 1,000 is just せん, without いち. But 10,000 is **いちまん**: here いち is required.
• **Sound changes** (memorize these five): **さんびゃく** (300), **ろっぴゃく** (600), **はっぴゃく** (800), **さんぜん** (3,000), **はっせん** (8,000). The rest are regular: よんひゃく, ななひゃく, きゅうひゃく, ろくせん, よんせん, きゅうせん.
• The big trap for English speakers: English groups big numbers by thousands (twenty thousand, a hundred thousand), but Japanese groups them by **10,000**. 20,000 is にまん (2 × 10,000), 50,000 is ごまん and 100,000 is **じゅうまん** (10 × 10,000).
• Tip: split off the last 4 digits. 36,500 → 3 | 6500 → さんまん + ろくせんごひゃく.
grammar.structure: [how many] + ひゃく / せん / まん, biggest unit first: にまん + さんぜん + ごひゃく = 23,500

examples.jp: とんかつは はっぴゃくえんです。
examples.kana: とんかつは はっぴゃくえんです。

examples.jp: この かさは さんぜんえんです。
examples.kana: この かさは さんぜんえんです。
examples.romaji: Kono kasa wa sanzen en desu.

examples.jp: この じてんしゃは にまんろくせんえんです。
examples.kana: この じてんしゃは にまんろくせんえんです。
examples.romaji: Kono jitensha wa niman rokusen en desu.

pitfalls: 10,000 is not まん on its own: まん ✗ → いちまん ✓. But 100 and 1,000 are just ひゃく and せん: いちひゃく ✗, いちせん ✗.
Don't count in thousands: にじゅうせん ✗ → にまん ✓ (20,000); ひゃくせん ✗ → じゅうまん ✓ (100,000).
300 is さんびゃく (さんひゃく ✗) and 3,000 is さんぜん (さんせん ✗). 600 is ろっぴゃく, but 6,000 is ろくせん, with no change.
400 is よんひゃく and 4,000 is よんせん: always よん, never し.
howToStudy: Write the five sound changes on a sticky note (さんびゃく, ろっぴゃく, はっぴゃく, さんぜん, はっせん) and read them aloud 5 times.
Take 5 prices from a store flyer or a website (just the number, ignore the currency) and say each one in Japanese, splitting off the last 4 digits.
Tap 🔬 on example 3: この shows up as DESCRIBES NEXT, じてんしゃは is the TOPIC, and the whole number (にまんろくせんえん) sits inside the PREDICATE, before です.

grammar.title: 〜えん · いくら
grammar.explanation:
The price is the **PREDICATE** of an X は Y です sentence: [thing] は [number]えんです。 To ask, **いくら** ("how much") goes exactly where the price goes: この さいふは いくらですか。— よんせんごひゃくえんです。
• The TOPIC is usually the thing you point at with この/その/あの or これ/それ/あれ (lesson 02-1). Read it starting from the predicate: "is 4,500 yen… this wallet".
• えん is the yen. Japanese has no "y" sound in it: say **en**, not "yen".
• えん is a **counter**, like じ and さい (lesson 01-2): it attaches straight to the number, and it has its own sound change. 4 yen is **よえん** (like よじ), but 40 yen is よんじゅうえん and 400 yen is よんひゃくえん.
• You may also hear なんえんですか ("how many yen?"); いくら is the most common.
grammar.structure: [thing] は いくらですか。— [number] えんです。

examples.jp: すみません、この さいふは いくらですか。— よんせんごひゃくえんです。
examples.kana: すみません、この さいふは いくらですか。— よんせんごひゃくえんです。
examples.romaji: Sumimasen, kono saifu wa ikura desu ka. — Yonsen gohyaku en desu.
examples.en: Excuse me, how much is this wallet? — It's 4,500 yen.

examples.jp: あの とけいは いくらですか。— いちまんにせんえんです。
examples.kana: あの とけいは いくらですか。— いちまんにせんえんです。
examples.romaji: Ano tokei wa ikura desu ka. — Ichiman nisen en desu.
examples.en: How much is that watch over there? — It's 12,000 yen.

examples.jp: その ぼうしは にせんろっぴゃくえんです。
examples.kana: その ぼうしは にせんろっぴゃくえんです。
examples.romaji: Sono bōshi wa nisen roppyaku en desu.

pitfalls: いくら doesn't take は: いくらは ✗. The thing takes は, and いくら goes at the end: 〜は いくらですか ✓.
English puts "how much" at the start of the question. In Japanese, いくら stays where the price will go, right before です: いくら この かさは ですか ✗ → この かさは いくらですか ✓.
えん has no "y" sound: "yen" ✗ → "en" ✓ (ごひゃくえん = gohyaku en).
4 yen is よえん, but 4,000 yen is よんせんえん: the よ reading only applies when the 4 sits right before えん.
howToStudy: Act out a dialogue by yourself, out loud, with 5 objects at home: ask 〜は いくらですか and answer with a made-up price.
Tap 🔬 on example 1: すみません is an INTERJECTION, この shows up as DESCRIBES NEXT, さいふは is the TOPIC and いくらですか is the PREDICATE. In the answer, the price takes the same place.
Tap 🔊 on example 2 and repeat along until you can say いちまんにせんえん without stumbling.

grammar.title: 〜を ください · 〜を おねがいします
grammar.explanation:
To ask for something, say **the thing + を + ください**: この かさを ください ("This umbrella, please" — in a shop, "I'll take this one"). **を** is the **OBJECT** label: like は, it comes right after its block and says what job the block has — here, the thing you want to receive. It is read **o**. ください is a polite "please give me", so it is the PREDICATE and goes at the end: Japanese puts the object **before** the verb, the reverse of English "give me this umbrella".
• **おねがいします** works the same way and sounds **softer**: とんかつを おねがいします ("A tonkatsu, please"). It's very common in restaurants and also works for services: メニューを おねがいします, おかいけい おねがいします ("The check, please").
• In speech, を is often dropped when the meaning is obvious: とんかつ、おねがいします。 The labels are still the norm, especially in writing.
• When you're handed something, you'll hear **どうぞ** ("here you are"). When you walk into a shop, you'll hear **いらっしゃいませ** ("welcome"); customers usually don't reply, and a small nod is enough.
• You'll study を with verbs in lesson 03-2.
• Going further (Sakubi): ください asks for something **for your benefit**. It also follows verbs, to ask someone to do something for you: みてください ("please look"). That uses the て-form, in lesson 06-2.
grammar.structure: [thing] を ください。 · [thing] を おねがいします。

examples.jp: じゃあ、この かさを ください。
examples.kana: じゃあ、この かさを ください。
examples.en: Well then, I'll take this umbrella. [lit. then, this umbrella, please give me]

examples.jp: すみません、とんかつを おねがいします。
examples.kana: すみません、とんかつを おねがいします。

examples.jp: メニューを おねがいします。— はい、どうぞ。
examples.kana: メニューを おねがいします。— はい、どうぞ。
examples.romaji: Menyū o onegai shimasu. — Hai, dōzo.
examples.en: The menu, please. — Sure, here you are.

pitfalls: を is read o, just like お: とんかつを = "tonkatsu wo" ✗ → "tonkatsu o" ✓. (You may hear "wo" in songs, but in speech it is o.)
The thing comes before the request: ください この かさ ✗ (the English order, "give me this umbrella") → この かさを ください ✓.
ください is not a loose "please" at the start of a sentence: ください、メニュー ✗ → メニューを ください ✓. To call a waiter or a clerk, use すみません.
"I want this" doesn't need a verb "want" (it comes in lessons 11-1 and 14-1). In a shop, これを ください says it all.
howToStudy: Make 5 requests out loud: 3 with ください (things in a shop) and 2 with おねがいします (in a restaurant).
Build it from the end, out loud: ください → かさを ください → この かさを ください. This fixes the Japanese order. Then tap 🔬 on example 1: かさを is the OBJECT and ください is the PREDICATE.
Record a complete shop dialogue (いらっしゃいませ → 〜は いくらですか → 〜えんです → じゃあ、〜を ください), doing both voices.

tasks.prompt: Write a 5-line shop dialogue: the clerk greets you, you ask the price of something, the clerk answers, you decide to buy it and the clerk hands it over. Then read it aloud, doing both voices.

items.q: Model (match its structure, not its words):

a.jp: いらっしゃいませ。— すみません、この かばんは いくらですか。— さんぜんはっぴゃくえんです。— じゃあ、これを ください。— はい、どうぞ。
a.romaji: Irasshaimase. — Sumimasen, kono kaban wa ikura desu ka. — Sanzen happyaku en desu. — Jā, kore o kudasai. — Hai, dōzo.
a.en: Welcome. — Excuse me, how much is this bag? — It's 3,800 yen. — Well then, I'll take this. — Sure, here you are.

items.note: Check: いくら and the price in the same predicate slot, the sound changes, and the thing before を ください.

practice.what: Play normally and read aloud, in Japanese, every number that appears on screen (money, items, points). If a line of dialogue has いくら, 〜えん, ください or おねがいします, pause and copy it into your notebook.
Drills → Numbers: 10 min — short daily sessions fix the five sound changes better than one long one. Then clear today's reviews and the Lesson 2 vocabulary in the SRS.
Practice L2: do the listening part, to understand numbers and prices said aloud.
Tap 🔊 on the examples in this lesson and repeat each price along with it, 3 times.

Open a Japanese online shop (search for くつ or ぼうし) and say the price of 10 products aloud in Japanese: just the number + えん. Try a pop-up dictionary such as Yomitan (a free browser add-on) on one product name: hover over it to see its reading and meaning. You won't understand the page yet, and that's fine — this is your first contact with real Japanese.

culture.title: Money: the little tray at the register, no tipping
culture.body: In many Japanese shops and restaurants there is a **small tray** next to the register, usually called a キャッシュトレー (cash tray); shop staff also call it カルトン. Instead of handing your money to the cashier, you put it on the tray; your change usually comes back into your hand or on the same tray, often with the bills counted in front of you. **Tipping is not part of the custom**: service is already included in the price, and money left on the table may make the staff think you forgot it. In many casual restaurants you pay at the register on your way out, not at the table. Coins go from 1 to 500 えん, and the most common bills are 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000 えん.
culture.try: Get a few coins and a small plate. Play the register: say the price in Japanese (せんにひゃくえんです。), put the money on the plate instead of handing it over, and say どうも when you get your change.

I can say numbers up to 100,000 counting in blocks of 10,000 (にまん, じゅうまん), without forgetting the いち in いちまん.
I can ask 〜は いくらですか。 and understand a price said aloud.
I can ask for something in a shop with 〜を ください.
I can order in a restaurant with 〜を おねがいします (a dish, the menu, the check).
